Biryar is a program that runs on your own computer. You use it in your
web browser, like a website, except that the website is on your own
machine and nobody else can open it.

Installing it is three lines typed once. After that it starts by itself.

## What you need

**A computer that stays on.** Biryar can only scan or reprice while the
computer it runs on is awake. A laptop works for trying it; for work that
should happen by itself, a small computer that is always on is better.
These are all fine:

| Machine | Notes |
|---|---|
| Windows 10 or 11 PC | 64-bit, with Docker Desktop |
| Mac | Intel or Apple chip, with Docker Desktop |
| Linux PC or home server | Docker Engine with the compose plugin |
| Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 | 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, 4 GB model or more |
| A small rented server | Any Linux with Docker; nothing else runs on it |

**What it uses.** Nothing you would notice on a computer from the last
ten years: about 1 GB of disk for the program and its database, around 300
MB of memory while running, two processor cores. **No graphics card**, no
second machine, no account with us. An internet connection, because it
reads Amazon and your retailers.

**Docker.** This is the one thing to install first. Docker is a free
program that runs other programs in a sealed box, so that Biryar brings
everything it needs and leaves the rest of your computer alone. Install
[Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) on Windows and Mac,
or Docker Engine on Linux. On Linux, if `docker ps` answers "permission
denied", add yourself to the `docker` group and sign in again.

## Run it

Open a terminal, which is a window you type commands into:

- **Windows:** press the Windows key, type `PowerShell`, press Enter. Make
  sure Docker Desktop is running first.
- **Mac:** press Command and Space together, type `Terminal`, press Enter.
- **Linux:** press Ctrl, Alt and T together.

Then paste these lines and press Enter. They make a folder, download one
small file into it, and start Biryar.

**Linux and Mac:**

```bash
mkdir biryar && cd biryar
curl -fsSLO https://biryar.ciyalabs.com/get/docker-compose.yml
docker compose up -d
```

**Windows** (it is `curl.exe`, not `curl`: PowerShell's own `curl` is a
different command):

```powershell
mkdir biryar; cd biryar
curl.exe -fsSLO https://biryar.ciyalabs.com/get/docker-compose.yml
docker compose up -d
```

That is all. The first start takes a minute, because the program is
downloaded and its database is set up. Then Biryar answers at
<http://localhost:8000>.

Remember the `biryar` folder. The commands on this page that begin with
`docker compose` have to be typed in it.

### After the machine restarts

You run those lines once. After a restart Biryar comes back by itself, at
the same address, as soon as Docker is running:

- **Linux**: Docker starts with the machine, and Biryar with it.
- **Windows and Mac**: Biryar starts when Docker Desktop does. To have that
  happen without opening it, switch on "Start Docker Desktop when you sign
  in" in Docker Desktop's settings, under General.

Give it a moment after switching on. Biryar waits for its database to
start before it answers, usually a few seconds. If the page still does not
open, `docker compose ps` in the `biryar` folder shows what is running, and
`docker compose up -d` there starts anything that is not.

## Your account

Open <http://localhost:8000> and choose **Sign up**. The first person to
sign up becomes the owner, and the page asks for this install's **setup
code**. Biryar printed it when it started. This shows it again:

```bash
docker compose logs api | grep -A 3 "setup code"
```

On Windows, in PowerShell:

```powershell
docker compose logs api | Select-String "setup code" -Context 0,3
```

The setup code is what makes the sign-up page safe. Without it, whoever
reached the page first would become the owner. With it, the owner is
someone who can already type a command on the computer Biryar runs on.

Then choose a username, give your email and choose a password: twelve
characters at least, with one that is not a letter or digit, and a capital
letter or a digit.

The next screen sets up **two-factor sign-in**. Scan the code on the
screen with an authenticator app on your phone (Google Authenticator,
Microsoft Authenticator, Aegis, 1Password and Bitwarden all work) and type
the six digits it shows. From then on, signing in is your password and a
code from the app. It is not optional: Biryar holds the keys to your
Amazon account, and Amazon asks for it on any system that holds its data.

Anyone else in the business joins with an **invitation code** you make
under **Settings, Team**. The code already says whether they are an owner
or an assistant.

Passwords last a year. Biryar warns two weeks ahead and asks for a new one
when the year is up.

## Your sealing key

On its first start Biryar makes the key that locks every Amazon and
service key it stores. There is nothing to generate and nothing to paste.
**Keep a copy somewhere that is not this computer:**

```bash
docker compose exec api cat /keys/sealing-key
```

That prints one line. Put it in your password manager, or on paper in a
drawer. Losing it means connecting Amazon again; anyone who has it, and a
copy of your database, can read what it locked.

## What to do next

Everything from here happens inside Biryar, on its screens. Nothing more
is typed into a terminal.

1. **Connect Amazon**, so Biryar can read your own seller account.
   [Connecting Amazon](/setup/sp-api/) walks through it with screenshots.
   Amazon reviews the request, so start this one first.
2. **Look at your figures** on the Portfolio page, and add what your
   products cost you. See [Portfolio](/guide/portfolio/). You can do this
   before Amazon is connected, with a statement downloaded from Seller
   Central.
3. **Add a Keepa key** if you want to look for deals, and a ScraperAPI key
   for the shops that need one. See [Keepa](/setup/keepa/) and
   [ScraperAPI](/setup/scraperapi/).
4. **Run a scan.** See [Sourcing](/guide/sourcing/).
5. **Watch the repricer decide**, and switch it on when you trust it. See
   [Repricing](/guide/repricing/).

## A forgotten password, or a lost phone

Nobody can email you a reset link, because Biryar runs on your computer
and not on ours. You get back in with one line typed on the computer
Biryar runs on:

```bash
docker exec -it biryar-api-1 biryar-password
```

It shows the accounts on that computer, asks which is yours, and lets you
choose a new password or have one made. It also covers a lost phone. There
is nothing in the line to change, and it works from any folder.
[Getting back into Biryar](/setup/getting-back-in/) goes through it step by
step, including what to do if you have never opened a terminal.

## Installing it as an app

Biryar is a web page served by your own computer, and it can be installed
like an app: in Chrome or Edge, **Install Biryar** from the address bar or
the menu; in Safari on a Mac, **File, Add to Dock**. It then has its own
icon and opens in its own window. Nothing extra is downloaded, and it
updates when Biryar does.

## Updating

In the `biryar` folder:

```bash
docker compose pull && docker compose up -d
```

Biryar brings its database up to date as it starts. An update that fails
changes nothing, and `docker compose logs api` says why.

## Backing up

Your data is on the computer Biryar runs on and nowhere else, so a backup
is yours to make. It is two things, both from the `biryar` folder.

The database, saved as one file:

```bash
docker compose exec db pg_dump -U biryar biryar > biryar-backup.sql
```

And the sealing key, without which the Amazon keys inside that file
cannot be read:

```bash
docker compose exec api cat /keys/sealing-key
```

Keep both somewhere that is not this computer.

## Moving to another computer

Install Biryar on the new computer, but before the first start put the
sealing key you saved in a file called `.env` beside `docker-compose.yml`:

```
BIRYAR_SECRET_KEY=v1:...
```

A key set in `.env` is used in place of the one Biryar would have made, so
the keys in your backup can be read on the new computer. Loading the
database file itself is a job for someone comfortable with PostgreSQL;
write to info@ciyalabs.com if you would like a hand with it.

## Settings you can change

None are needed. A file called `.env` beside `docker-compose.yml` can
change the port Biryar answers on, or keep it on one version. The example
at <https://biryar.ciyalabs.com/get/env.example> lists every line with
what it does.

The most common one: if something else on the computer already uses port
8000, put `BIRYAR_PORT=8001` in `.env` and start again. Biryar then
answers at <http://localhost:8001>.

## Less common tasks

These are for someone comfortable in a terminal. Most installs never need
them.

**Print the setup code on request:**

```bash
docker compose run --rm api python -m biryar.init --setup-code
```

**Make the owner without the sign-up page.** This prints a generated
password, shown once:

```bash
docker compose run --rm api python -m biryar.init --email you@example.com
```

**Stay on one version.** In `.env`, `BIRYAR_VERSION=latest` follows new
releases, and a number such as `BIRYAR_VERSION=0.1.0` stays on that
release until you change it.

**Undo a database update**, should a release ever need undoing. Every
update has a tested way back:

```bash
docker compose run --rm api alembic downgrade -1
```

**Change the sealing key.** Put the new key first and keep the old one, in
`.env`:

```
BIRYAR_SECRET_KEY=v2:<new>,v1:<old>
```

Stored keys move to the new sealing key as they are next used. Nothing has
to be redone in one go and nothing stops working meanwhile. Drop the old
key once everything has moved.

**How it is put together.** Biryar is three parts that the one file
starts together: the program you see, a worker that does the reading and
pricing in the background, and a PostgreSQL database. The program never
uses the database's owner account, so the rules that keep one business's
records apart from another's always apply to it.
